selection.method: highest remaining verified actor-primary profiles after Batch 21

profiles.name: Jay Reel
profiles.excerpt: Jay Reel helped create, produce and perform Chet Chetter’s Tales from the Morgue, a later audio-drama series shaped by the traditions of classic radio.
profiles.bio_html:
Jay Reel developed Chet Chetter's Tales from the Morgue with longtime collaborator Mark Sawyer through M&J Audio Theater. The project grew from homemade audio drama into a professionally distributed series influenced by older radio programs such as X Minus One, Lum and Abner and Gunsmoke.

Reel was not only a performer. He co-created and produced the series and supplied multiple recurring voices, including Chet Chetter and Elmer Korn. Those creative and production responsibilities make writing/creation and producing genuine parts of his profile alongside voice performance.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 19 Chet Chetter's Tales from the Morgue performances credited to Reel, documenting a later generation of audio drama consciously built from classic-radio storytelling traditions.

profiles.name: Larry Robinson
profiles.excerpt: Larry Robinson was a New York radio repertory actor whose surviving work bridges experimental drama, science fiction, Johnny Dollar and Theater Five.
profiles.bio_html:
Larry Robinson worked in the New York radio repertory during the final decades of network dramatic broadcasting. His credits show a performer moving among anthology drama, detective stories and science fiction rather than depending on one continuing role.

Robinson appeared repeatedly on Theater Five and also worked on Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, Columbia Workshop and X Minus One. That span connects the experimental network tradition of the 1940s and 1950s with radio drama's 1960s revival efforts.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten Theater Five performances credited to Robinson, three Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances, two each on Columbia Workshop and X Minus One, and one CBS Radio Mystery Theater performance.

profiles.name: Leone LeDoux
profiles.excerpt: Leone LeDoux was a versatile radio actress and voice performer whose career ranged from Lux Radio Theatre and Blondie to the voice of Minnie Mouse.
profiles.bio_html:
Leone LeDoux built a career in radio and voice performance during the 1930s through the 1950s. Her microphone work included dramatic anthology, family comedy and character voices, giving her a range that extended well beyond a single program.

LeDoux appeared repeatedly on Lux Radio Theatre and Blondie, with additional work on My Favorite Husband and Screen Directors Playhouse. She also voiced Minnie Mouse during part of the character's early sound era, placing her inside the history of animation voice performance as well as radio.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves eight Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to LeDoux, four Blondie appearances, two each on My Favorite Husband and Screen Directors Playhouse, plus additional dramatic work.

profiles.name: Ransom Sherman
profiles.excerpt: Ransom Sherman was a radio comic, writer and host whose career stretched from Club Matinee and Hap Hazard to a recurring role on Fibber McGee and Molly.
profiles.bio_html:
Ransom Sherman was born in Appleton, Wisconsin in 1898 and entered radio after earlier work in sales and music. He became a major Chicago broadcasting personality, developing a style built on ad-lib comedy, monologues and relaxed audience contact.

Sherman hosted Club Matinee, starred in and wrote Hap Hazard, and later worked across radio and television as a comic actor and master of ceremonies. His writing and hosting were substantial parts of his profession, not side credits.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 19 Fibber McGee and Molly performances credited to Sherman and one Duffy's Tavern appearance, while his wider career places him among radio's notable actor-writer-host personalities.

profiles.name: Bill Smith
profiles.excerpt: Bill Smith was a radio repertory actor whose surviving credits cross comedy, mystery, crime and science fiction from Fibber McGee and Molly to Johnny Dollar.
profiles.bio_html:
Bill Smith is best documented through the broadcasts themselves, where his name appears across several very different network series. The record shows a working repertory performer rather than a star tied to one program.

Smith moved among comedy on Fibber McGee and Molly, supernatural drama on The Mysterious Traveler, crime on Gang Busters and detective work on Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar. That range is the clearest measure of his radio career.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves four performances each on Fibber McGee and Molly and The Mysterious Traveler credited to Smith, three each on Gang Busters and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, two The Chase appearances and additional anthology work.

profiles.name: Bruce Payne
profiles.excerpt: Bruce Payne was a supporting radio actor whose surviving work is concentrated in Lux Radio Theatre, with additional literary and suspense drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Bruce Payne belongs to the supporting company of actors heard repeatedly in Hollywood network drama. His surviving radio credits place him around major stars and feature adaptations rather than in one continuing character role.

Lux Radio Theatre became the strongest concentration of Payne's work, supplemented by NBC University Theater, Escape, The Railroad Hour and The Whistler. Those programs required dependable actors who could establish a new supporting part quickly inside highly produced broadcasts.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 11 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Payne, three NBC University Theater appearances, two Escape episodes and additional work on The Railroad Hour and The Whistler.

profiles.name: Celeste Rush
profiles.excerpt: Celeste Rush was a regular Lux Radio Theatre supporting actress whose eighteen surviving GRH performances place her inside the program’s Hollywood stock company.
profiles.bio_html:
Celeste Rush is best documented through Lux Radio Theatre, where weekly adaptations of major films depended on a dependable supporting company surrounding the featured stars. Her repeated credits show sustained professional work rather than a single guest appearance.

Actors in the Lux company often handled several smaller characters in one production and had to match the pace and polish of performers arriving from the film studios. Rush's recurring presence reflects the trust placed in those stock players to make each adaptation sound fully populated.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 18 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Rush, providing a concentrated record of her contribution to one of network radio's most ambitious dramatic series.

profiles.name: Colleen Collins
profiles.excerpt: Colleen Collins was a West Coast radio actress whose surviving work crosses Fibber McGee and Molly, Lux Radio Theatre, westerns and crime drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Colleen Collins worked in the Hollywood radio repertory across comedy, anthology drama, westerns and crime programs. Her cast record shows the broad professional flexibility expected of supporting actresses during the network era.

Collins appeared most often in Fibber McGee and Molly, while Lux Radio Theatre, Escape, Tales of the Texas Rangers, The Saint and This Is Your FBI placed her in very different dramatic settings.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves eight Fibber McGee and Molly performances credited to Collins, three Lux Radio Theatre appearances and additional broadcasts across six other dramatic and musical series.

profiles.name: Dix Davis
profiles.excerpt: Dix Davis became one of radio’s notable child actors as Randolph on A Date with Judy before leaving performance for a long career in intelligence analysis.
profiles.bio_html:
Dixon Davis was born in Los Angeles in 1926 and entered film and radio as a child. He became best known on the air as Randolph, Judy Foster's quick-witted younger brother on A Date with Judy, one of the era's popular teenage comedies.

Davis also worked on Lux Radio Theatre and other programs while still young, but acting did not become his lifelong profession. After higher education he moved into government service and spent decades as an intelligence analyst, making his radio career a distinct early chapter of his life.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Davis, five A Date with Judy appearances and an additional Dr. Christian broadcast.

profiles.name: Don Randolph
profiles.excerpt: Donald Randolph brought Broadway training and a resonant stage voice into American radio, where he became a dependable player in literary, mystery and suspense drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Donald Randolph was born in Cape Town, South Africa in 1906 and established himself on Broadway during the 1930s. His stage career included Shakespeare, contemporary drama and musical theatre before film, radio and television broadened his work.

Randolph's resonant voice made him a natural radio character actor. He appeared on NBC University Theater, Let George Do It, The Adventures of Philip Marlowe, The Mysterious Traveler and The Whistler, moving easily between literary adaptation and genre drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven NBC University Theater performances credited to Randolph, two each on four mystery and detective series, and additional work on Lux Radio Theatre, The Railroad Hour and The Sealed Book.
